nameStory: The cockatiel gets its name from its distinctive crest of feathers that can be raised and lowered like a cockerel's comb. The name combines 'cockatoo' (referring to its family) with the diminutive suffix '-iel,' essentially meaning 'little cockatoo.' In Australia, they're also called 'weero' or 'quarrion,' names that mimic their distinctive whistling calls.
description: The cockatiel is a medium-sized parrot with a graceful, slender build and a prominent feather crest on its head. These Australian natives are about the size of a small dove, with long pointed wings and a distinctive long, tapered tail. Wild cockatiels have gray bodies with bright orange-red cheek patches, white wing bars, and yellow heads and crests (especially prominent in males). As popular pet birds, you might encounter escaped or released individuals in various color mutations including white, yellow, or pied patterns.

idTips.label: Distinctive crest
idTips.description: A tall, pointed crest of feathers on the head that moves expressively up and down - when alert or excited, the crest stands straight up like a mohawk, but when calm or frightened, it lies flat against the back of the head

idTips.label: Orange cheek patches
idTips.description: Bright orange-red circular patches on both sides of the head that look like painted-on blush circles - these are most vibrant in males and can appear almost flame-colored in good light

idTips.label: Long pointed tail
idTips.description: A distinctive long, narrow tail that tapers to a point and makes up about half the bird's total length - feels stiff and is often held at an angle when perched

idTips.label: Whistling calls
idTips.description: Clear, melodic whistles and warbling sounds that carry well - often includes repetitive phrases or wolf-whistle-like notes that sound almost human

idTips.label: Sleek gray body
idTips.description: Smooth, pearl-gray plumage on the body and wings with crisp white patches on the wing coverts that flash conspicuously in flight

habitat: In New England, cockatiels are not wild residents but may occasionally be spotted as escaped pet birds in suburban and urban areas. Look for them near bird feeders, in parks with large trees, or perched on telephone wires and rooftops where they might seek food and shelter. They may temporarily join flocks of other seed-eating birds but cannot survive New England winters outdoors.

seasonality.spring: Escaped pet cockatiels are most likely to be spotted in spring as people begin opening windows and spending more time outdoors with their pets, creating opportunities for accidental escapes.
seasonality.summer: The warmest season offers the best survival conditions for any escaped birds, when they might be seen at bird feeders or foraging in gardens for seeds and fruits.
seasonality.fall: Any escaped cockatiels become increasingly desperate for food sources and may be more approachable or vocal as they struggle to find adequate nutrition before cold weather arrives.
seasonality.winter: Cockatiels cannot survive New England winters outdoors and any sightings would likely be birds in immediate distress requiring rescue, or indoor birds viewed through windows.

funFact: Cockatiels are one of the few parrot species where you can tell the gender just by looking - males have bright yellow faces and vibrant orange cheek patches, while females have grayish faces with more muted orange cheeks, and only the males sing complex songs to attract mates!
confusionNotes: Escaped cockatiels might be confused with mourning doves due to their similar size and gray coloring, but cockatiels have that unmistakable pointed crest, bright orange cheek patches, and much more upright perching posture. Remember: if it has a punk-rock crest and orange 'blush,' it's a cockatiel!
contextualKnowledge: While cockatiels are extremely popular pet birds worldwide, they are native only to Australia and any individuals seen in New England are escaped or released pets that cannot establish breeding populations in our climate. These sightings often represent birds in need of rescue, as domestically-raised cockatiels lack the survival skills of their wild counterparts.
compareHints: Cockatiels are unique within the cockatoo family for their sleek build and long tail - most other cockatoos are stockier, shorter-tailed birds with much larger, more curved crests. While cockatiels are the smallest members of the cockatoo family, they're easily distinguished from other small parrots by their distinctive pointed crest that no other parrot species possesses. Their elegant proportions and that mobile crest make them unmistakable among pet birds.
